summary.text: Acting for Megan Hughes (claimant), this brief addresses 2 issue(s) arising from Hughes v PeakFit Ltd: Ms Hughes wants to enforce PeakFit's promise to pay £2,000 as a binding contract and claim the money.
Did PeakFit Ltd intend to create legal relations, or was the promise a mere puff? Favourable for Megan Hughes.
Was PeakFit Ltd's communication a binding offer, rather than an invitation to treat, which Megan Hughes accepted? Unfavourable for Megan Hughes.

facts.text: On 5 January 2025 PeakFit published an advertisement on its website and social media: "Complete all 100 daily PeakFit workouts by 15 April and if you have not lost 5 kg we will pay you £2,000. We have placed £100,000 with Northgate Bank to show we mean it."
The advertisement said participants must log every workout in the app and weigh in on the app's connected scales on 15 April.
Ms Hughes downloaded the app on 6 January 2025, paid the £9.99 subscription, logged all 100 workouts and weighed in on 15 April 2025, having lost only 1.2 kg.

On 20 April 2025 she emailed PeakFit claiming £2,000. PeakFit replied that the advertisement was a marketing promotion and only an invitation to treat, that it never accepted her as a participant, and that she should have told it when she started.
PeakFit's general terms say that promotions "may be withdrawn at any time". PeakFit did not withdraw this promotion before 15 April 2025.
More than 3,000 people downloaded the app during the promotion. PeakFit says it never expected to be legally bound to pay all of them and that the advertisement was obvious marketing puff.

issues.question: Did PeakFit Ltd intend to create legal relations, or was the promise a mere puff?

proposition.text: When spouses are not living in amity the presumption against intention to create legal relations does not apply, and written terms point towards an intention to be bound.

supporting_precedents.case_name: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co

proposition.text: An advertisement can be an offer where its terms are clear and it shows an intention to be bound by anyone who performs the conditions.
In domestic and social agreements there is a presumption that the parties do not intend to be legally bound.

supporting_argument.text: Merritt v Merritt [1970] 1 WLR 1211 supports Megan Hughes on this issue: When spouses are not living in amity the presumption against intention to create legal relations does not apply, and written terms point towards an intention to be bound. That reasoning applies here: More than 3,000 people downloaded the app during the promotion. Balfour v Balfour is distinguishable on its facts: A husband working in Ceylon promised to pay his wife 30 pounds a month while she remained in England for health reasons. By contrast, in this case: PeakFit's general terms say that promotions "may be withdrawn at any time". PeakFit did not withdraw this promotion before 15 April 2025.

opposing_argument.text: Balfour v Balfour [1919] 2 KB 571 supports PeakFit Ltd on this issue: In domestic and social agreements there is a presumption that the parties do not intend to be legally bound. That reasoning applies here: More than 3,000 people downloaded the app during the promotion. PeakFit says it never expected to be legally bound to pay all of them and that the advertisement was obvious marketing puff.

assessment.text: Favourable: the authorities on balance support Megan Hughes, led by Merritt v Merritt; Balfour v Balfour is the main authority the other side will rely on.

issues.question: Was PeakFit Ltd's communication a binding offer, rather than an invitation to treat, which Megan Hughes accepted?

supporting_precedents.case_name: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co

proposition.text: An advertisement can be an offer where its terms are clear and it shows an intention to be bound by anyone who performs the conditions.
Advertisements of goods for sale are ordinarily invitations to treat rather than offers, because the advertiser has limited stock and cannot sensibly be bound to sell to everyone who replies.

opposing_precedents.case_name: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd

proposition.text: Displaying goods with prices invites customers to make offers; the seller remains free to accept or refuse each offer.
Goods displayed in a shop window with a price attached are an invitation to treat; the customer makes the offer.
